title: Biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE, and their blood supply

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to rebuild the living tissue responsible for sharp central vision after its light-sensing cells have died. A successful treatment would establish a durable mosaic of cone photoreceptors in a degenerated human macula, give those cells functional light-sensitive outer segments, and connect them appropriately to surviving host bipolar cells so that their signals can enter the existing visual pathway.

The cones would also need adequate support from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), the underlying Bruch’s membrane, and the choriocapillaris blood supply. The RPE helps transport nutrients from the choroid and remove photoreceptor debris. Reconstruction therefore concerns a functioning tissue system, rather than simply placing new light-sensitive cells in the eye. Which supporting layers require replacement or repair would depend on the recipient’s lesion; the supplied evidence does not establish that every patient needs all of them rebuilt.

The intended route could involve transplantation, regeneration within the eye, or a combination. Its defining outcome would be biological phototransduction and useful central vision attributable to reconstructed tissue. Survival of an RPE graft alone would establish a narrower achievement, while an electronic implant would provide a different mechanism of vision restoration.

significance.text: Geographic atrophy destroys macular photoreceptors, and advanced inherited retinal diseases can also cause irreversible retinal cell loss. Existing approaches include anti-VEGF treatment for neovascular AMD and complement inhibition intended to slow geographic atrophy. Durable reconstruction would add the ability to repair some central vision loss after cells have died, rather than relying solely on preserving remaining tissue or substituting an artificial signal. The supplied evidence does not document an achieved reconstruction of a naturally functioning human fovea.

The disease burden makes that possibility consequential. In a news release dated 5 May 2013, NEI described advanced AMD as the leading cause of blindness in the United States; this is a historical attribution, not an updated ranking for every population. The supplied WHO fact sheet, dated 10 February 2026, attributes approximately 8 million cases of distance vision impairment or blindness to AMD. That number describes disease burden and cannot be treated as the population eligible for foveal reconstruction.

Conditional impact synthesis: clinically useful reading under natural light would demonstrate an important new capacity for biological central-vision repair. It would not, by itself, establish normal color discrimination, adaptation to changing illumination, normal foveal resolution, or restoration of the entire visual field. Describing central vision loss as a repairable tissue injury would be justified only for the diseases, lesions, and functional outcomes actually demonstrated. Extension to widespread retinal degeneration would remain a further possibility requiring additional evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is coordinated survival and functional integration of replacement or regenerated cones in a diseased human macula. NEI describes humans as having little, if any, capacity to replace lost retinal neurons. Producing retinal cells is therefore only an intermediate step: the cells must persist, form functioning outer segments, and establish appropriate connections with host circuitry. Anatomical survival without usable signal transmission would leave the main reconstruction goal unmet.

A second barrier is sustaining the reconstructed tissue. Adequate RPE function and metabolic support from the choroid must accompany the cones, with repair of damaged support structures where necessary. Immune rejection and resource-intensive cell production are documented challenges. The original research also identifies scarring as a possible obstacle, but the supplied review does not directly substantiate a specific graft-scarring mechanism or its frequency; it remains a concern to investigate rather than an established explanation for failure.

Engineering synthesis: the treatment would have to coordinate cell identity, spatial organization, delivery, tissue support, and circuit integration in the same recipient. It would also need to establish which downstream retinal pathways remain usable in advanced disease. Success in a small central graft would not automatically solve manufacturing, delivery, immune management, or integration across a much larger retinal area.

current_state.text: NEI’s AGI projects describe work on survival and integration of regenerated retinal cells, including photoreceptors, against the background of very limited natural neuronal replacement in humans. Cavaleri and colleagues’ 2025 review characterizes visual improvements across neurorestoration approaches as generally modest and notes reliance on small preliminary studies and potential bias. That assessment is a broad expert judgment, not a standardized quantitative comparison with normal macular vision. Its included studies extend through September 2025; the supplied extraction is truncated in the references, although the relevant narrative passages were available to the reviewer.

The supplied research attributes to Heier and colleagues’ OAKS and DERBY report, dated 21 October 2023, approximately 16–22% less geographic-atrophy growth with pegcetacoplan at 24 months and no difference in the key secondary visual-function endpoints at that time. These numerical and endpoint details remain unconfirmed within the supplied evidence because the retained article copy contains only redirect text. They should be read as reported research details pending verification, not as disproven findings. The broader distinction between slowing atrophy and rebuilding lost photoreceptors is supported by the supplied PRIMA manuscript.

The supplied research describes Rao and colleagues’ report, dated 6 November 2025, as an adult RPE-stem-cell graft study involving six people, with low-dose safety findings and a mean gain of 21.67 letters at 12 months in the three worse-seeing eyes. It also describes the trial as not powered for efficacy and as not rebuilding cones. The retained source contains only redirect text, so the participant count, safety interpretation, subgroup result, statistical-power statement, and cone-reconstruction conclusion cannot be confirmed here. Even if the reported visual gain is verified, an RPE intervention would require additional evidence before it could establish reconstruction of a functional cone mosaic.

The supplied research attributes to Hirami and colleagues’ report, dated 7 December 2023, survival of allogeneic retinal-organoid sheets for two years in two people with retinitis pigmentosa, with a possible light-response change in one participant. The retained article copy contains only redirect text, leaving those trial-specific details unconfirmed. The reported distinction remains scientifically important: persistence of transplanted tissue and a possible light response would be partial achievements, rather than evidence of reconstructed foveal reading vision.

A clearer demonstrated comparator is the PRIMA prosthesis in the supplied Holz and colleagues author manuscript, published online on 20 October 2025. Its pixels convert projected near-infrared light into electrical stimulation of surviving bipolar cells. Mean unenhanced prosthetic acuity was 1.32 ± 0.16 logMAR, approximately Snellen 20/417, consistent with the sampling limit of its 100 µm pixels. At 12 months, 26 of 32 assessed participants improved by at least 0.2 logMAR relative to baseline; 38 participants had been enrolled. The system-assisted testing allowed adjustable zoom and brightness, so that improvement should not be equated with native implant resolution. The system uses camera-equipped glasses and near-infrared projection. These results demonstrate electronic substitution, not biological cone replacement. The supplied review assessed the main manuscript prose; its figures and linked supplements were not inspected.

The supplied research also cites Ho’s 2024 IOVS conference abstract 2137 for approximately 0.3 logMAR improvement from count-fingers baselines after optogenetic bipolar-cell therapy. No abstract text was captured, so the magnitude, baseline characterization, and trial details cannot be confirmed from the supplied materials. This is a conference-level report in the research record, not a reviewed full clinical report here. The record does not establish whether a full peer-reviewed RESTORE report was available by 1 November 2026.

The evidence supports a landscape of partial biological approaches and demonstrated prosthetic function, while leaving the integrated reconstruction goal unachieved in the supplied record. It does not establish a complete treatment or approval inventory as of 1 November 2026. Although the supplied primary PRIMA manuscript extends beyond the review’s September 2025 study cutoff, the empty freshness record prevents a confident claim that all subsequent developments have been captured.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in patients with fovea-involving geographic atrophy or an end-stage macular dystrophy and suitable surviving downstream circuitry, a cell or regeneration therapy would produce photoreceptor outer segments, a measurable cone response attributable to the reconstructed tissue, and clinically useful reading under natural light without an electronic implant or intensifying goggles. Acuity, reading performance, illumination conditions, safety outcomes, and a multiyear durability interval should be defined prospectively. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Reconstructed cones enable clinically useful reading under natural light

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal and anatomical evidence: demonstrate benefit against an appropriate control, using an untreated fellow eye only where its disease course and other characteristics make it a suitable comparator. Combine functional outcomes with evidence of graft or regenerated-cell persistence, host-circuit integration, and adequate RPE and metabolic support. Functional improvement alone would not establish every anatomical component named in the concept, while anatomical survival alone would not establish useful vision. RPE survival and prosthetic pixels would each fall short of the integrated biological outcome.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled visual benefit with persistent, integrated tissue and RPE support

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the outcome across patients and independent clinical teams, with consistent manufacturing or regeneration methods and follow-up sufficient to assess durability and immune complications. Report the lesions, retained circuitry, treatment burden, and safety conditions under which benefit occurs. Claims about restored color vision or adaptation require dedicated tests. Successful finite trials would establish breadth within the tested population and conditions, rather than universal applicability across macular diseases or proof that full-field replacement is feasible.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible patient outcomes across independent teams with reported treatment boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: OPH-11, “Prevention of progression from early or intermediate AMD to late AMD,” addresses disease progression before the advanced tissue-loss state targeted here. OPH-07, “One programmable repair for many photoreceptor and RPE gene defects,” addresses genetic repair. Its overlap with OPH-02 could include protecting or correcting cells used in reconstruction, but gene correction in surviving native cells would not itself replace an already lost cone mosaic. These relationships follow the supplied titles and research framing; detailed definitions of OPH-07 and OPH-11 were not independently established.

Roster-based distinction: OPH-08, “Reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout,” overlaps with the need for adequate blood supply, but retinal capillary reperfusion and reconstruction of choriocapillaris support beneath the RPE are different anatomical targets. OPH-01, “Retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion cell axons to brain targets,” concerns the output pathway beyond the photoreceptors and bipolar cells. OPH-10, “Arrest of glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the lever,” concerns preservation of that downstream neuronal population. These capabilities could matter when damage extends beyond the outer retina, but none alone establishes foveal cone reconstruction.

Roster-based distinction: OPH-05, “Patterned vision from the brain when the eye cannot send signals,” seeks visual function through a different intervention site. OPH-09, “Reopening of the human visual critical period,” concerns neural plasticity, which could be relevant to learning to use restored retinal signals but would not itself supply missing retinal tissue. PRIMA and optogenetic bipolar-cell approaches likewise illustrate alternative routes to visual function rather than completion of OPH-02.

Roster-based distinction: OPH-03, “Reversal of established cataract without removing the lens,” and OPH-04, “A manufactured cornea that clears vascularized stromal opacity,” target optical barriers in front of the retina. OPH-06, “A closed-loop control that sets axial eye growth,” targets ocular growth. They address different causes of impaired vision and remain separate innovations. Full-field photoreceptor replacement in widespread retinitis pigmentosa shares OPH-02’s underlying reconstruction biology, while adding substantial scale, delivery, manufacturing, and integration requirements.

unresolved_issues: The Heier, Rao, and Hirami numerical findings and trial-specific interpretations require article or abstract content beyond the retained redirect text; Ho’s abstract was not captured.

The recommendation to remove the unconfirmed trial details was not adopted wholesale. They were retained as clearly qualified reports to preserve useful quantitative research detail without presenting it as verified.
The record cannot establish whether a full peer-reviewed RESTORE report or other material developments were available by 1 November 2026; the supplied freshness record is empty.
The lesion-specific need to replace RPE, Bruch’s membrane, or choriocapillaris, and the minimum surviving downstream circuitry needed for benefit, remain to be determined.
The specific importance and mechanism of graft scarring are not directly substantiated by the supplied evidence.
Clinically useful acuity, reading performance, acceptable treatment burden, and the required multiyear durability interval remain proposed criteria needing prospective operational definitions.
The eligible treatment population cannot be inferred from WHO’s AMD burden estimate, and detailed definitions of related roster entries extend beyond the supplied titles and research framing.

brief.title: Living tissue repair for lost central vision
possible: People who have lost sharp central vision could read again under natural light. Treatment would rebuild cones, the eye’s light-sensing cells for fine detail, connect them to surviving nerve cells, and provide the supporting tissue and blood supply they need.
why: For people with advanced age-related macular degeneration or inherited diseases that destroy central vision, this would add a way to repair damage after cells have died. Existing treatments largely aim to preserve the tissue that remains.

sources.showed: Its research programme includes models for testing whether regenerated light-sensing cells survive and connect to existing nerve pathways.
sources.cited_for: Replacement cells must survive and connect to the eye’s remaining nerve pathways.
sources.not_established: The programme description does not demonstrate restored human central vision.

sources.showed: Their review found modest visual improvements across approaches to restoring vision. Much of the clinical work involves small preliminary studies.
sources.quote: Although the methods discussed above have shown promise individually, improvements in vision have been modest at best.
sources.cited_for: Current approaches have produced partial gains rather than full biological reconstruction.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish useful central vision from rebuilt cones and their supporting tissue.

sources.showed: Adding omega-3 fatty acids to the tested nutritional supplement combination did not improve protection against age-related macular degeneration.
sources.quote: Adding omega-3 fatty acids or lowering zinc to the AREDS formulation also had no effect on AMD progression.
sources.cited_for: Age-related macular degeneration destroys tissue needed for reading and other tasks requiring sharp central vision.
sources.not_established: The supplement study concerns disease progression, not replacement of lost light-sensing cells.

sources.showed: Its estimates attribute about 8 million cases of distance vision impairment or blindness to age-related macular degeneration.
sources.quote: The leading causes of vision impairment and blindness are refractive errors and cataracts.
sources.cited_for: Age-related macular degeneration contributes substantially to vision loss worldwide.
sources.not_established: Disease burden does not establish how many people could benefit from central vision reconstruction.

sources.showed: This is a clinical report on pegcetacoplan, a drug intended to slow geographic atrophy, the progressive loss of central retinal tissue.
sources.cited_for: Slowing tissue loss is a different achievement from rebuilding lost light-sensing cells.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish biological reconstruction of central vision.

sources.showed: This is a small human study of stem-cell grafts for the retinal pigment epithelium, the cell layer that nourishes light-sensing cells and removes their debris.
sources.cited_for: Replacing the supporting cell layer is one component of biological repair.
sources.not_established: A supporting-cell graft does not establish a functioning arrangement of replacement cones.

sources.showed: This is a small human study transplanting sheets of lab-grown retinal tissue into people with retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys light-sensing cells.
sources.cited_for: Transplanted retinal tissue is a partial biological approach to replacing lost cells.
sources.not_established: Surviving transplanted tissue does not establish useful reading through rebuilt central vision.

sources.showed: In a small clinical study, the PRIMA electronic implant improved central visual sharpness with camera-equipped glasses. Testing allowed adjustable magnification and brightness.
sources.quote: There was no significant change in peripheral natural VA compared to baseline.
sources.cited_for: Surviving retinal pathways can carry useful signals generated by an electronic implant.
sources.not_established: Electronic stimulation does not establish biological light sensing by replacement cones.

sources.showed: This is a conference report on therapy that makes surviving retinal relay cells sensitive to light.
sources.cited_for: Making surviving cells light-sensitive offers another route to visual function.
sources.not_established: This approach does not establish replacement of cones and their supporting tissue.

shown: Hirami and colleagues have reported survival of transplanted sheets of lab-grown retinal tissue. Rao and colleagues have studied grafts of the supporting cell layer. These small human studies have not established useful reading from rebuilt cones.

Holz and colleagues demonstrated improved central vision with the PRIMA electronic implant and camera-equipped glasses. That shows useful signals can pass through surviving retinal pathways, but biological reconstruction remains unachieved.
missing: Replacement cones must survive, develop working light-sensitive parts, and connect to surviving nerve cells in a diseased human eye.
Rebuilt tissue must receive lasting nourishment and waste removal, with damaged supporting layers and blood supply repaired where needed.
Controlled trials must link useful, lasting central vision to the reconstructed tissue.
Independent teams must reproduce the benefit while managing immune rejection and producing consistent treatment.

milestones.label: Rebuilt cones support useful reading in natural light
milestones.explanation: Rebuilt cones would have to develop working light-sensitive parts and produce measurable responses supporting lasting, useful reading under natural light without electronic aids. This would establish biological central vision repair.

milestones.label: Controlled benefit accompanies connected, supported living tissue
milestones.explanation: A controlled trial would have to show visual benefit alongside persistent cells, connections to host nerves, and adequate nourishment from supporting tissue. This would link useful vision to an integrated biological repair.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce benefits within defined treatment boundaries
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce durable benefits across patients using consistent methods and report eligible damage, surviving pathways, treatment burden and safety. This would establish where treatment works reliably.

uncertain: Which supporting layers need repair, and how much surviving nerve circuitry is enough for useful vision?
What reading ability, treatment burden and duration of benefit should count as clinical success?
Would restored reading also bring useful colour vision and adaptation to changing light?

page.title: Cone photoreceptor replacement for central vision restoration
page.definition: Replacement or regenerated cones, the light-sensing cells used for fine central vision, restore signals through surviving circuits in the human macula, the central retina. The cells receive support from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), its underlying Bruch’s membrane and the choroidal blood supply, with damaged supporting tissue repaired where required.

goal.need: WHO’s fact sheet of 10 February 2026 attributes 8 million cases of distance vision impairment or blindness to age-related macular degeneration. NEI identifies retinal neuron loss as a cause of irreversible blindness and states that humans have little capacity to replace these cells. Replacing lost cones addresses vision lost after cell death; the burden estimate does not measure treatment eligibility.

statements.body: National Eye Institute, Audacious Goals Initiative
statements.quote: to restore vision through regeneration of neurons and neural connections in the eye and visual system.
statements.context: The programme targets retinal neurons; its photoreceptor work includes replacement and regeneration.

statements.quote: OpCT-001 aims to restore vision in patients with primary photoreceptor diseases by replacing degenerated cells in the retina with functional cells.
statements.context: OpCT-001 is an investigational cell therapy derived from induced pluripotent stem cells.

completion.title: Replacement or regenerated cones cause restored central vision in a human retina.
completion.criterion: In a person whose central vision was lost through cone death, demonstrate surviving replacement or regenerated cones that convert visible light into electrical signals, transmit those signals to host retinal neurons and cause measurable improvement in central visual function. Establish functioning tissue support, preserving or repairing RPE, Bruch’s membrane and choroidal supply as required by the lesion. Distinguish new-cone function from rescue of surviving cells and electronic stimulation. No numerical acuity, reading-speed or durability threshold is asserted.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, applying NEI’s regenerative-vision goal to central cone replacement; no external integrated completion test was located.
completion.basis: Searches of NEI AGI reports, FDA retinal and cell-therapy guidance, photoreceptor trial endpoints and published consensus criteria found no completion test for combined foveal cone, RPE and vascular reconstruction. NEI asks whether a new cell is “present, connected, and transmitting visual information.” This fallback requires causal human visual restoration without adding an unsupported numerical cutoff.

milestones.title: Laboratory-grown human cones generate intrinsic electrical responses to light.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate cone identity and light-driven electrical function, rather than photoreceptor markers alone. Saha et al., published online on 31 January 2022, recorded intrinsic light responses in approximately 35% of more than 100 cones sampled across retinal organoids from four human stem-cell lines. The laboratory result establishes cellular function, not repair of either disease class.
milestones.set_by: NEI AGI Photoreceptor Regeneration and Integration Workshop, published in 2015; its functional-capacity criterion is qualitative.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstration of New Photoreceptor Authenticity and Functional Capacity

milestones.title: Transplanted cones transmit light-driven signals to host retinal neurons in an animal model.
milestones.criterion: Show functional transmission from transplanted cones into host retinal circuitry. Ribeiro et al., published on 20 April 2021, assessed retinal electrophysiology three months after transplantation in six mice receiving functional human cones, five receiving nonfunctional cones and five untreated degeneration controls. Restored responses depended on synaptic transmission. The rd1 model represents inherited degeneration; rodents lack a fovea.
milestones.set_by: NEI AGI Photoreceptor Regeneration and Integration Workshop, published in 2015; its synaptogenesis criterion specifies no universal response magnitude.
milestones.threshold_quote: promoting synaptogenesis of transplanted cells to restore light-driven signals.

milestones.title: Preclinical evidence supports an authorised human photoreceptor-replacement trial.
milestones.criterion: Product-specific preclinical studies support the conclusion that the proposed human investigation is reasonably safe. In the United States, the investigational new drug application takes effect after 30 days without a clinical hold, or on earlier FDA notification. For inherited photoreceptor disease, BlueRock announced OpCT-001 clearance on 3 September 2024 and its first CLARICO treatment on 8 July 2025. These sponsor reports are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, early-phase cellular and gene therapy guidance, section III.C, and 21 CFR 312.40; these are general requirements rather than cone-specific numerical thresholds.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations

milestones.title: Transplanted photoreceptor tissue survives for one year in a human retina.
milestones.criterion: Establish graft survival and safety through the first year after retinal-sheet transplantation. Hirami et al., published on 7 December 2023, reported stable graft survival for two years without serious adverse events in two people with advanced retinitis pigmentosa. For dry AMD, an earlier fetal retina–RPE study reported no clinical rejection and one-year graft imaging. Neither result establishes functioning replacement foveal cones.
milestones.set_by: Kobe City Eye Hospital’s iRERP protocol, jRCTa050200027, as reported by Hirami et al.; the one-year endpoint was written for iPSC-derived retinal sheets in retinitis pigmentosa.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary endpoint was the survival and safety of the transplanted retinal organoid sheets in the first year post-transplantation.

milestones.title: Retinal replacement preserves or improves human visual acuity after one year.
milestones.criterion: At one year, preserve or improve acuity on the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study letter chart, tested at 85 cd/m². This was the fetal retina–RPE study’s success criterion, not a universal threshold. Published online on 10 June 2008, its nonrandomized study of 10 people reported improvement in three of six with retinitis pigmentosa and four of four with dry AMD. It had no control group; visual improvement did not establish donor-cone causation.
milestones.set_by: Radtke et al., phase II fetal retina–RPE transplantation study, Methods: Study Design; written for retinitis pigmentosa and dry AMD.
milestones.threshold_quote: Success was defined as preservation or improvement of vision after one year as measured by EDTRS.

not_found: No human report was verified that demonstrates restored central vision caused by replacement cones transmitting signals into host retinal circuitry.
The iRERP registry page could not be opened; its primary endpoint was available in the peer-reviewed clinical report.
The CLARICO ClinicalTrials.gov page exposed no study text; a registry mirror was readable.
The supplied OAKS/DERBY, RPESC-RPE, PRIMA and Ho conference URLs did not provide readable article or abstract text.

results.finding: Human retinal organoid cones: 36 of 107 responded to light.
results.detail: Cone identity was supported by morphology and cone-specific proteins. Responses were measured without added external chromophore; suppression experiments suggested minimal contribution from neighboring cones. This laboratory result does not demonstrate disease repair.

results.finding: In six rd1 mouse retinas receiving human cones, 52% ± 9% of recorded units were light-responsive.
results.detail: Retinas were assessed three months after transplantation. Light-evoked spiking was reversibly inhibited by glutamatergic synaptic blockers; nonfunctional-cone and untreated controls showed little response.
results.quote: This provides strong evidence that these responses originate from transplanted cones and are transmitted via a glutamatergic synapse between human cones and murine host BCs.

results.finding: In 4 aged rd1 mouse retinas receiving human cone transplants, 54.2% of recorded units were light-responsive.
results.detail: Untreated rd1 controls had 2.5% light-responsive units (3 retinas). Synaptic blockers reversibly eliminated fast light responses in transplanted retinas, supporting transmission to host retinal neurons.

results.finding: In four primate eyes with human retinal organoid grafts, two showed ON-bipolar responses improved by up to 21.6%.
results.detail: Cone-rich grafts formed synaptic contacts with host bipolar cells, but the electrophysiology did not isolate signals from transplanted cones or directly establish transmission through those contacts. The model used acute laser-induced macular damage rather than progressive age-related macular degeneration.
results.quote: Nevertheless, b-wave increases of 17.5%–21.6% in the current study were remarkably stable across longitudinal assessments, supporting their physiological relevance.
